The article doesn't really cite any evidence that the TOR network is fundamentally flawed or compromised - no, really, it doesn't. Only in the title. Its blog-style links that look like they'd go to stories about the "compromise" or the "hack" go to the Wikipedia page on TOR, and the TOR project homepage.

Read Wikipedia's page on the "weaknesses" and be reassured that all of them rely on either controlling or disabling a large amount of exit nodes, or on people who are using the network using it improperly, such as with applications that do not use TOR well, or with other applications NOT on TOR. If the TOR network is healthy and you are only running well-designed applications and all of your network traffic is going through TOR, you're fine. It's not a magic invisibility cloak, it is a tool that has to be used properly or else it does not work... RTFM.

Granted, there is not an easy way for the laymen to check the overall health or innocence of the TOR network, but ostensibly that will become less of an issue as people realize the importance of the network and contribute more innocent exit nodes.

How much does it cost to run an exit node? You could stack a load of virtual nodes on each physical server so your only real costs are for the IP addresses, which I don't think governments have trouble obtaining. If running a million TOR nodes is enough to compromise the network (and I bet far fewer would do it) then I guarantee that at least one agency has a million nodes sitting in their basement.

http://tor.stackexchange.com/questions/113/how-does-a-tor-client-pick-tor-nodes-for-circuit-creation

It's unlikely that a bunch of virtual nodes sitting on the same physical machine in the same physical location would consistently get picked to route your traffic - the client side route selection is set up to spread out over different IP addresses. To circumvent this with a slew of virtual nodes in one place, IANA would have to be in on it, and issue millions of IP addresses that did not conform to their stated policy and existing precedent.

While not impossible, this would stick out. I don't know what it takes to get the TOR network to decide that a node is a known "bad "node, but I have to imagine that a failure to adhere to the IP addressing standard that the rest of the Internet depends on would be on the checklist.

If nothing else, it is harder to control and monitor TOR traffic than normal Internet traffic. In the age where we know that the US government, at least, is demanding private keys from certificate authorities and seeking once again to prohibit end-to-end encrypted systems (which for the average citizen are still vulnerable to lead-pipe cryptography), and even willing and able confiscate a foreign national's property in the name of enforcement of US law, it may very well be that it is impossible to have a truly secure interaction over the Internet.

To fault enhanced privacy or security measures for no reason other than that a nationstate attacker can theoretically bypass them, in certain circumstances, is naïve. TOR Is still a very strong choice for people desiring increased privacy and anonymity online.
